skill_title: Apply the photoelectric effect (work function, threshold frequency, max KE)
notes: 20 items: 13 lifted, 7 fresh. Photoelectric effect definition + calculations: E = hf, W₀ = hf₀, E_k(max) = hf − W₀; threshold frequency; effects of intensity vs frequency.

items.question: Define the PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT.
items.expectedAnswer: The photoelectric effect is the process whereby electrons are ejected from the surface of a metal when electromagnetic radiation of sufficient frequency (above the threshold) shines on it.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'electrons ejected from metal surface' + 'EM radiation of sufficient frequency'.

items.question: Define the WORK FUNCTION of a metal.
items.expectedAnswer: The work function (W₀) is the MINIMUM energy needed to eject an electron from the surface of a metal.
items.explanation: Two marks: 'minimum energy' + 'eject electron from surface'. W₀ = h × f₀ (threshold frequency).

items.question: A photon has energy E. If the frequency of the photon is doubled, its energy becomes:
items.explanation: E = hf — energy is directly proportional to frequency. Doubling f doubles E.

items.question: A photon has energy 2X joules. The work function of the metal is X joules. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected photoelectron?
items.explanation: E_k(max) = E_photon − W₀ = 2X − X = X J.

items.question: The threshold frequency of a metal is f₀. If light of frequency 2f₀ shines on the surface, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons is:
items.explanation: E_k = hf − W₀ = h(2f₀) − hf₀ = hf₀.

items.question: The photoelectric effect is best explained by treating light as:
items.explanation: Einstein's photon model: light is quantised into discrete packets (photons) of energy hf. The wave model alone cannot explain the threshold-frequency dependence.

items.question: Which phenomenon provides evidence that LIGHT has a PARTICLE nature?
items.explanation: Photoelectric effect shows light comes in quanta (photons). Diffraction, interference and refraction all support the wave nature.

items.question: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz shines on a zinc surface (W₀ = 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). Calculate the energy of ONE photon of the incident light. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.)
Continuing: photon energy = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, W₀ (zinc) = 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons OR explain if none are emitted.
items.expectedAnswer: E_k = E_photon − W₀ = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ = −1.58 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. A negative result means the photon energy is LESS than the work function. So NO photoelectrons are emitted. The light frequency is below the threshold frequency of zinc.
items.explanation: If hf < W₀, no electrons are emitted at all. Negative 'KE' is unphysical — the answer is 'no emission'.

items.question: Calculate the threshold frequency of zinc (W₀ = 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s).
The intensity of light incident on a metal surface (above threshold) is DOUBLED. What is the effect on the MAXIMUM KINETIC ENERGY of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.expectedAnswer: E_k(max) REMAINS THE SAME. Intensity determines the NUMBER of photons per second (and hence the number of electrons emitted per second), but each electron absorbs only ONE photon. The maximum KE depends only on the frequency of the light (E_k = hf − W₀), not on intensity.
items.explanation: Critical concept. Intensity controls electron NUMBER; frequency controls electron ENERGY.

items.question: Caesium is illuminated with light of wavelength λ = 4.7 × 10⁻⁷ m. The threshold frequency of caesium f₀ = 4.37 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the maximum speed of the ejected photoelectrons. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴, c = 3 × 10⁸, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.)
Light of frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz is incident on a metal with W₀ = 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the maximum SPEED of the photoelectrons. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴, m_e = 9.11×10⁻³¹.)
The threshold frequency for metal A is 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the work function of metal A. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.)

In a photoelectric experiment with light above threshold frequency: if the INTENSITY of the light is INCREASED (at the same frequency), what happens to the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons?
items.explanation: Intensity does NOT affect E_k(max). Only frequency does.

items.question: Continuing: if the INTENSITY is increased at the same frequency, what happens to the NUMBER OF PHOTOELECTRONS ejected per second?
items.explanation: Higher intensity ⇒ more photons per second ⇒ more electrons ejected per second.

items.question: Light of frequency 1.2 × 10¹⁵ Hz shines on a metal. The total energy absorbed by the metal per second is 1.75 × 10⁻⁹ J. Calculate the NUMBER of photons per second incident on the metal. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴.)
UV light shines on a negatively-charged zinc plate in an electroscope. Explain why the gold leaf COLLAPSES.
items.expectedAnswer: UV photons have frequency above the threshold frequency of zinc, so they have enough energy to eject electrons from the zinc plate (photoelectric effect). The negatively-charged plate progressively loses electrons, reducing its negative charge. As the plate becomes less negative, the gold leaf is less repelled and FALLS BACK toward the stem (collapses).
items.explanation: UV ⇒ photoelectrons ejected ⇒ plate loses negative charge ⇒ less repulsion ⇒ leaf falls.

items.question: If GREEN light (at higher intensity than the original UV) replaces the UV on the same zinc electroscope, will the leaf collapse? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: NO. Green light has a LOWER frequency than UV, BELOW the threshold frequency of zinc. No photoelectric emission occurs, no matter how intense the green light is. Higher intensity provides more photons but each photon still has insufficient energy individually (hf < W₀). The leaf will not collapse.
items.explanation: Frequency is what matters for ejection. Below threshold ⇒ no emission, regardless of intensity.

items.question: On a graph of E_k(max) (y-axis) versus frequency f (x-axis) for a photoelectric experiment with a given metal, what do (a) the gradient, (b) the x-intercept, and (c) the y-intercept represent?
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Gradient = Planck's constant h ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. (b) x-intercept = threshold frequency f₀ (where E_k = 0). (c) y-intercept = −W₀ (the negative of the work function; the line is E_k = hf − W₀, so when f = 0, E_k = −W₀ — but this part of the graph is unphysical because no emission occurs below f₀).
items.explanation: E_k = hf − W₀ ⇒ linear graph with gradient h and x-intercept f₀.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_PE_DEFINITION: Photoelectric effect definition missing 'electrons from surface' or 'sufficient frequency'
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WORK_FUNCTION_DEF: Work function definition incomplete (minimum energy / surface)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_EK_MAX_FORMULA: Wrong formula for E_k(max) = hf − W₀
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_PHOTON_PARTICLE_NATURE: Doesn't connect photoelectric effect to particle (photon) nature
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_NEGATIVE_KE: Reports a negative E_k as a valid emission energy
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_INTENSITY_VS_NUMBER: Doesn't link intensity to number of photoelectrons
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_WAVELENGTH_FREQUENCY: Misuses c = fλ when converting between λ and f
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_PHOTON_COUNTING: Wrong photon-count from total energy / energy per photon
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_PE_ELECTROSCOPE: Can't link photoelectron emission to electroscope behaviour
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_FREQUENCY_THRESHOLD: Doesn't recognise frequency below threshold means no emission
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_EK_F_GRAPH_GRADIENT: Doesn't recognise gradient of E_k-vs-f graph equals h
